title: The best of stories
hookLine: We tell you the best of stories (12:3)

lines: WE TELL YOU THE BEST OF STORIES.
cards: Surah Hud ended with prophet after prophet, and people after people who would not listen. It's heavy. The next surah opens differently, like someone settling into a chair by the fire.
We tell you, it says, the best of stories. You've met Yusuf already on this path: the dream of the eleven stars, the well, the prison, the palace. Now, back to him with a different question.
Not what happens. Why does this surah open by speaking of the best of stories?

teach.b: Verse three, in Pickthall's translation, begins: "We narrate unto thee (Muhammad) the best of narratives". In Arabic, ahsan al-qasas.
Qasas can mean the stories themselves or the act of telling them, so commentators read it both ways: the best of stories, or the best way of telling.
They also differ on what it points to: the story of Yusuf that follows, or the Qur'an's telling as a whole.
Some commentators place the surah in a hard stretch of the Prophet's years in Mecca, around the time he lost his wife Khadija and his uncle Abu Talib, with the small community under heavy pressure.

And here is a story about a boy betrayed by his brothers, sold, slandered, jailed, forgotten, who ends up with power over the very people who wronged him. So what makes it best? Commentators give answers that stack.
It's complete: one prophet's story told from beginning to end in a single surah.

teach.h: EVERY KIND OF PERSON, EVERY TRIAL.
teach.b: It has every kind of person: prophets and kings, a jealous family, a woman who tries to seduce and later confesses, a prisoner, a merchant, a grieving father.
It has every kind of trial: envy, temptation, injustice, long separation, grief that whitens a father's eyes.
And it ends not in destruction, like the stories in Hud, but in a family reunited and a sentence of forgiveness.
When the brothers finally stand before him, Yusuf says: no reproach on you today.
The best of stories is the one where the wronged man, with all the power in the room, chooses mercy.

how: Surah Yusuf is often retold; parents tell it to children, and teachers use it to speak about patience, temptation and forgiveness within families.

o: the oldest stories, handed down before the prophets
the longest of all the stories in the Qur'an
the best of stories, or the best way of telling

p: the best of stories, or of telling

games.q: you're Yusuf, now powerful in Egypt. the brothers who threw you in a well stand before you, ashamed. what do you say?
o: now you'll know how it felt.
games.why: no reproach on you today; may God forgive you. the wronged man with all the power chooses mercy (12:92).

practice: Run Yusuf's story in five pictures, one per breath: the dream, the well, the prison, the palace, the brothers bowing. Then go back to the picture you feel most, and stay with it a while.
Let it end where Yusuf ends it: no reproach on you today.

wordCard.voice: Ahsan al-qasas. The phrase that opens the story of Yusuf, read as the best of stories or the best way of telling.

orig.note: Arabic: "the best of stories" (12:3); qasas is both the stories and the telling.

carryVoice: Your line: no reproach on you today. Said by the man holding all the power. Thanks for sitting with me.
